item.title: - What illuminates the world? What awakens the world? Who works together with humans? What is their conduct? Who nourishes both the lazy and the…
item.description:
- What illuminates the world?
What awakens the world?
Who works together with humans?
What is their conduct?
Who nourishes both the lazy and the diligent,
Like a mother her child?
What beings sustain their lives
Depending on the earth?
- Wisdom illuminates the world,
Right mindfulness awakens the world,
Cattle work together with humans,
The plough is their path.
Rain nourishes both the lazy and the diligent,
Like a mother her child.
Rain sustains beings' lives,
Depending on the earth.

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 1.80

item.title: And, bhikkhus, what is the practice of restraint? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu, when seeing a form with the eye, does not grasp the general sign,…
item.description:
And, bhikkhus, what is the practice of restraint? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu, when seeing a form with the eye, does not grasp the general sign, does not grasp the particular sign. For whatever reason, if the eye faculty were unrestrained, covetousness, grief, evil unwholesome states might arise, he restrains that cause, guards the eye faculty, practices the restraint of the eye faculty. When he hears a sound with the ear... smells an odor with the nose... tastes a taste with the tongue... feels a touch with the body... cognizes a mind-object with the mind, he does not grasp the general sign, does not grasp the particular sign. For whatever reason, if the mind faculty were unrestrained, covetousness, grief, evil unwholesome states might arise, he restrains that cause, guards the mind faculty, practices the restraint of the mind faculty. This, bhikkhus, is called the practice of restraint.

From: Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.164

item.title: The Blessed One: Like a bull breaking its bonds, Like an elephant tearing rotten creepers, I will not enter a womb again. So if you…
item.description:
The Blessed One:
Like a bull breaking its bonds,
Like an elephant tearing rotten creepers,
I will not enter a womb again.
So if you wish, O deva of rain, let it rain!

From: Sutta Nipāta 1.2

item.title: And, bhikkhus, what is adherence to local language and excessive use of everyday speech? Here, bhikkhus, in various regions, people know words for 'dish', 'bowl',…
item.description:
And, bhikkhus, what is adherence to local language and excessive use of everyday speech? Here, bhikkhus, in various regions, people know words for 'dish', 'bowl', 'cup', 'plate', 'pot', 'basin', 'vessel'. Thus, as they know these words in those regions, someone insists, clings, and says: 'Only this is true; everything else is false.' Thus, bhikkhus, is adherence to local language and excessive use of everyday speech. And, bhikkhus, what is non-adherence to local language and non-excessive use of everyday speech? Here, bhikkhus, in various regions, people know words for 'dish', 'bowl', 'cup', 'plate', 'pot', 'basin', 'vessel'. Thus, as they know these words in those regions, a person, without clinging, explains: 'They, depending on this, speak thus.' Thus, bhikkhus, is non-adherence to local language and non-excessive use of everyday speech.

From: Majjhima Nikāya 139 – Araṇavibhaṅgasutta

item.title: Bhikkhus, if one were to speak rightly about Sāriputta, one could say: 'Sāriputta is the legitimate son of the Blessed One, born of his mouth,…
item.description:
Bhikkhus, if one were to speak rightly about Sāriputta, one could say: 'Sāriputta is the legitimate son of the Blessed One, born of his mouth, born of the Dhamma, fashioned by the Dhamma, an heir of the Dhamma, not an heir of material things.'

From: Majjhima Nikāya 111 – Anupadasutta

item.title: Reflecting wisely, he uses lodging only to ward off cold, to ward off heat, to ward off the touch of flies, mosquitoes, wind, sun, and…
item.description:
Reflecting wisely, he uses lodging only to ward off cold, to ward off heat, to ward off the touch of flies, mosquitoes, wind, sun, and creeping things, only to remove the dangers of climate, and only for the purpose of seclusion and quietude.
Reflecting wisely, he uses medicines and medical requisites only to ward off arisen painful feelings and for the sake of complete freedom from affliction.
Bhikkhus, if he did not use thus, harmful, afflicting taints might arise; but when he uses thus, those harmful, afflicting taints do not arise. These, bhikkhus, are called taints that are to be abandoned by using.

From: Majjhima Nikāya 2 – Sabbāsavasutta

item.title: 'One who clings, bhikkhu, is bound by Māra. One who does not cling is freed from the Evil One.' - 'Venerable Sir, I understand. Well-Gone…
item.description:
'One who clings, bhikkhu, is bound by Māra. One who does not cling is freed from the Evil One.' - 'Venerable Sir, I understand. Well-Gone Sir, I understand.' - 'How, bhikkhu, do you understand in detail the meaning of my brief statement?' - 'Venerable Sir, one who clings to form is bound by Māra. One who does not cling is freed from the Evil One. One who clings to feeling ... to perception ... to formations ... to consciousness is bound by Māra. One who does not cling is freed from the Evil One. Venerable Sir, this is how I understand in detail the meaning of the Blessed One's brief statement.' - 'Good, good, bhikkhu! It is good that you understand thus the meaning of my brief statement. One who clings to form, bhikkhu, is bound by Māra. One who does not cling is freed from the Evil One. One who clings to feeling ... to perception ... to formations ... to consciousness is bound by Māra. One who does not cling is freed from the Evil One.'

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 22.63

item.title: And, bhikkhus, how is mindfulness of breathing developed and cultivated so as to perfect the four foundations of mindfulness? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu goes to…
item.description:
And, bhikkhus, how is mindfulness of breathing developed and cultivated so as to perfect the four foundations of mindfulness? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu goes to the forest, to the root of a tree, or to an empty hut, sits down, folding his legs crosswise, keeping his body straight, and establishing mindfulness in front of him. Mindfully he breathes in, mindfully he breathes out ... 'Contemplating relinquishment, I will breathe in,' he trains; 'Contemplating relinquishment, I will breathe out,' he trains. Whenever, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu breathing in long understands: 'I breathe in long'; or breathing out long, he understands: 'I breathe out long' ... breathing in short, he understands: 'I breathe in short'; breathing out short, he understands: 'I breathe out short' ... 'Experiencing the whole body, I will breathe in,' he trains ... 'Tranquilizing the bodily formation, I will breathe in,' he trains; 'Tranquilizing the bodily formation, I will breathe out,' he trains. At that time, bhikkhus, dwelling contemplating the body as a body, a bhikkhu abides ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world. Why is that? Bhikkhus, I say that this is a certain body, namely, in-breath and out-breath. Therefore, bhikkhus, at that time, dwelling contemplating the body as a body, a bhikkhu abides ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world.

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 54.16

item.title: Just as, sisters, a skilled butcher or his apprentice, after killing a cow, cuts it up with a sharp butcher's knife without damaging the inner…
item.description:
Just as, sisters, a skilled butcher or his apprentice, after killing a cow, cuts it up with a sharp butcher's knife without damaging the inner flesh or the outer skin, and then cuts, severs, and removes all the inner sinews, inner tendons, and inner ligaments. After cutting, severing, and removing them, and after removing the outer skin, he covers the cow again with that same skin and says: 'This cow is attached to this skin as before' — would that person be speaking correctly?" "No, venerable sir." "Why is that?" "Even though, venerable sir, that skilled butcher or his apprentice, after killing the cow ... covers it again with that same skin, he could say: 'This cow is attached to this skin as before' — but the cow is already separated from that skin." "I give this simile, sisters, to convey the meaning. The meaning here is this: 'Inner flesh' is a synonym for the six internal bases. 'Outer skin' is a synonym for the six external bases. 'Inner sinews, inner tendons, inner ligaments' are a synonym for desire and lust and greed. 'The sharp butcher's knife' is a synonym for noble wisdom. With that noble wisdom, he cuts, severs, and removes the inner defilements, inner fetters, inner bonds.

From: Majjhima Nikāya 146 – Nandakovādasutta

item.title: Bhikkhus, with these words, the mind of the Blessed One Vipassī, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, inclined towards inaction, to passivity, not wishing to…
item.description:
Bhikkhus, with these words, the mind of the Blessed One Vipassī, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, inclined towards inaction, to passivity, not wishing to teach the Dhamma. Then a certain Great Brahmā, having known with his mind the thought of the Blessed One Vipassī, thought: 'Alas, the world will be destroyed, the world will perish, if the mind of the Blessed One Vipassī, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, inclines towards inaction, to passivity, not wishing to teach the Dhamma!' Bhikkhus, that Great Brahmā, just as a strong man might stretch his bent arm or bend his outstretched arm, vanished from the Brahmā world and appeared before the Blessed One Vipassī, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One. Bhikkhus, then the Great Brahmā arranged his upper robe on one shoulder, knelt on his right knee on the ground, saluted the Blessed One Vipassī with joined palms, and said: 'Venerable Sir, let the Blessed One teach the Dhamma! Let the Well-Gone teach the Dhamma! There are beings with little dust in their eyes who will be lost if they do not hear the Dhamma. Having heard, they will understand the Dhamma.'

From: Dīgha Nikāya 14 – Mahāpadānasutta
